notes.meaning: Jesus traveled to Jerusalem for one of the Jewish festivals, showing His obedience to God's law. Scripture does not specify which feast this was, but the event gave Jesus an opportunity to reach large crowds. His visit set the stage for important teaching about who He is.

In Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate stood a pool called Bethesda, which means house of mercy. It was surrounded by five covered walkways where people could rest. These porches offered shelter right beside the city where many came to worship.

A great crowd of sick, blind, lame, and paralyzed people lay along the walkways. They gathered there because they hoped to receive healing for their physical ailments. Their helplessness showed how desperately they needed help.

People believed that an angel came down to stir the pool water at certain times. The first person to step in after the water moved was said to be completely cured. Traditional teachers saw this as a special work of God to show mercy to His people before Christ came.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Most ancient Greek manuscripts do not contain this verse, showing it was likely an early note added by scribes to explain the belief mentioned in verse seven.

notes.meaning: Among the crowd was a man who had suffered from a disabling illness for thirty-eight years. He had endured this condition for almost a lifetime and had no human way to fix it. His long struggle highlights how deep his suffering was.

Jesus saw the man lying there and already knew he had been sick for a very long time. He asked him if he wanted to get well, awakening the man's hope and focusing his attention. The question invited the man to look for God's help rather than giving up.

The sick man replied that he had no friend to carry him into the water when it was stirred. Every time he tried to crawl toward the pool, someone else stepped in before him. He was completely dependent on others, yet no one was there to assist him.

Jesus told the man to stand up, pick up his sleeping mat, and walk. Even though the man could not walk on his own, the power of Christ went with the command. True faith responds by trusting Jesus and taking action at His word.

The man was healed at once, lifted his mat, and began to walk normally. This miracle proved Christ's power to restore strength in an instant. John notes that this happened on the Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest, which soon sparked fierce opposition.

Religious leaders confronted the healed man and said it was against the law to carry a mat on the Sabbath. They were guarding man-made traditions about what counted as work on God's holy day. Instead of rejoicing that a paralyzed man could walk, they focused entirely on their rules.

The man answered that the very person who healed him told him to pick up his mat and walk. He reasoned that someone with the power to perform such a miracle had full authority to tell him what to do. He trusted the word of the healer over the complaints of the leaders.

The leaders asked him who told him to carry his mat, completely ignoring the fact that he was cured. They did not care about the wonderful work of mercy that had taken place. Their only interest was finding someone to blame for breaking their Sabbath rules.

The healed man did not know who Jesus was because Jesus had quickly slipped away into the crowd. Jesus chose to leave quietly rather than create a scene or draw unnecessary attention. He was not seeking public applause for His miracle.

Jesus later found the man at the temple and told him to stop sinning so that nothing worse would happen to him. While sickness is not always caused by personal sin, Jesus warned that turning back to a sinful life brings terrible consequences. God's mercy calls us to live in grateful obedience.

The man went and told the religious leaders that Jesus was the one who had healed him. He pointed to Jesus as the source of his new health, likely trying to honor his healer or explain himself to the authorities. His report quickly turned the leaders' attention toward Jesus.

The Jewish leaders began to persecute Jesus because He healed people on the Sabbath day. They treated His acts of kindness as crimes against God's law. Their anger blinded them to the clear evidence that God was working through Him.

Jesus defended Himself by stating that His Father is always at work caring for creation, and He works alongside Him. God never stops doing good or sustaining life on the Sabbath, and Jesus shared that same divine authority. Doing good on the Sabbath reflects the very heart of God.

These words made the leaders even more eager to kill Jesus. They saw that He not only ignored their Sabbath rules, but also called God His own Father in a unique way. By doing this, He was clearly claiming to be equal with God.

Jesus told them that the Son cannot act on His own apart from the Father, but does whatever He sees the Father doing. This shows that Jesus is not a rival to God, but is in perfect union with Him. The Father and the Son share the same divine nature and work together as one.

Jesus explained that the Father loves the Son and reveals everything He is doing to Him. He promised that the Father would show Him even greater works that would leave the leaders amazed. These coming works would display God's supreme authority even more clearly.

Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, the Son also gives life to whomever He pleases. Only God possesses the power over life and death. By claiming this authority, Jesus declared that He has the divine power to give both physical life and new spiritual life.

Jesus added that the Father does not judge anyone directly, but has handed all judgment over to the Son. Judging all humanity requires total knowledge of every person's heart and actions. Entrusting this authority to Jesus shows that He holds the place of God Himself.

The Father gave Jesus this role so that all people would honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Anyone who refuses to give worship and honor to Jesus fails to honor God who sent Him. We cannot truly love or worship God while rejecting His Son.

Jesus promised that whoever listens to His word and trusts in the Father has eternal life right now. Such a person will not face final judgment or punishment, because they have already passed out of spiritual death into life. Faith in Christ brings complete security in God's saving grace.

differ.view: True believers have crossed permanently from death to life and will persevere to the end without ever losing their salvation.
Believers possess eternal life now, but this promise does not prevent falling into condemnation if one abandons faith in Christ.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Eternal life is received through faith, but it is not an unconditional guarantee; a believer who turns away from faith can forfeit life and come under judgment.
